paragraphs: Some days are worth putting on the calendar, and Mordecai knew it. He asked the Jews to keep two days every year, the days their "sorrow turned to joy" (Esther 9:22). He wanted these days remembered by every generation, so that "the memory of them" would not "fade from their descendants" (Esther 9:28). Friend, I can walk into my own pantry and forget why I came in, so I respect a man who builds a whole holiday so nobody forgets.

Look at HOW they were told to celebrate: with feasting, joy, "sending gifts to one another and to the poor" (Esther 9:22). Joy was never meant to stay in your own cookie box. A blessing you keep to yourself goes stale, and a blessing you pass along gets fresher. So when good days come for you, baker, remember them on purpose, and let somebody else taste the sweetness too.

Then the passage shows us what Mordecai did with his greatness. He was "second only to King Xerxes," and still he was "seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen" (Esther 10:3). Power, a promotion, a bigger seat at the table: all of it is for the whole batch, not just the one holding it. Whatever you've been handed, baker, ask who it can help, and then go help them.
